beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string (DOCUMENTDB_URI) from an environment variable at runtime and never commit it to source control or write it to logs; use Azure Key Vault or another secret store in production.
Enable TLS/SSL and certificate validation on the Mongo/Motor client (e.g., tls=true, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=false) when connecting to the Azure DocumentDB Mongo endpoint.
Create a single Motor/MongoClient and reuse it application-wide (do not create a client per request); attach Beanie to that single async client at startup and close it on shutdown.

Tune connection-pool and timeout settings for expected concurrency (maxPoolSize / minPoolSize, socketTimeoutMS, serverSelectionTimeoutMS) rather than accepting defaults in high-concurrency async apps.
Use Motor (async pymongo driver) under Beanie for async access rather than creating blocking pymongo clients or synchronous DB calls in async code.
Use a least-privilege database user/role scoped to the application database (sample_retail_19) instead of using a cluster admin credential in the app.
Model unordered product pairs with a canonical key (e.g., 'pair_key' = min(productA, productB) + '_' + max(productA, productB)) so each unordered pair is stored exactly once.

Use a dedicated 'product_pairs' collection that stores: canonical_pair_key (unique), product_ids array, embedding vector (float array), co_purchase_count, and standard metadata (created_at, updated_at).
Create a unique index on the canonical_pair_key to allow atomic upserts (update with upsert: true) when incrementing co-purchase counts and writing/overwriting embeddings.

Create a vector index on the embedding field with appropriate algorithm and metric (e.g., HNSW with cosine or inner product) so approximate nearest-neighbor queries run efficiently instead of scanning all documents.
Store vectors as dense float32 arrays and normalize vectors when you plan to use cosine similarity; persist dimension metadata and validate vector length on writes.
Batch embedding requests to OpenAI (or whichever embedding service) and cache embeddings for already-seen pairs to avoid repeated external API calls and rate-limit errors.
When creating vector indexes, tune index parameters (e.g., M, efConstruction, efSearch, nlist depending on algorithm) according to the target recall vs latency and test with realistic queries.

For the cross-sell endpoint, perform a vector nearest-neighbor search to get candidate product pairs and then re-rank candidates by a deterministic affinity formula (e.g., weighted combination of normalized co_purchase_count and vector similarity).

Use MongoDB aggregation pipelines server-side to aggregate order history into co-purchase counts (unwind products, self-join/group to compute unordered pairs) rather than fetching all orders to the application.
Increment co-purchase counts atomically with update operators ($inc) and use upsert to create pair docs if they do not exist, avoiding race conditions during concurrent updates.
Implement exponential backoff and retry logic for transient MongoDB and network errors (e.g., MongoNetworkError, PrimaryStepDown) and make repeated writes idempotent where possible.
Set reasonable query time limits (maxTimeMS) for aggregation and vector search operations and enforce request cancellation/timeouts from the FastAPI layer to avoid resource exhaustion.
Do not store sensitive PII in embeddings or metadata; if product identifiers are sensitive, store hashed/opaque IDs and keep mapping in a separate secure store.
Create conventional indexes to support non-vector filters and sorting (e.g., index on co_purchase_count, product_ids elements) so hybrid queries that filter by metadata remain efficient.
Build indexes online or in background where possible and avoid blocking the cluster with large index builds in production; schedule heavy index operations during low-traffic windows.
Monitor index usage, slow queries and vector index metrics (recall/latency) and use explain() and built-in monitoring tools to validate that queries use the intended indexes.

When provisioning for vector workloads, ensure the cluster compute tier and storage are sized for ANN indexes and memory needs (ANN indexes often require large memory and IO), and plan to scale up if searches are slow or resource-bound.
Validate and enforce embedding dimension and numeric type at write time (schema validation or application checks) to prevent corrupt or wrong-length vectors from breaking vector index queries.
When returning recommendations, paginate results, apply query-level limits, and avoid returning raw embedding data; return only product IDs, scores, and necessary metadata.
